objectives: Reason about power, thermal, comms budgets.

slides.title: Subsystems of a spacecraft
slides.body:
A spacecraft is a tightly integrated system. Major subsystems:

**Structure**: physical chassis. Light + rigid. Aluminum (older), composite (modern). Carries loads from launch + microgravity ops.

**Propulsion**: maneuvering + station-keeping. Chemical (large $\Delta v$, station-keeping), ion (long missions). Reaction control system (RCS) thrusters for attitude.

**Attitude Determination + Control System (ADCS)**: keep spacecraft pointed.
- **Sensors**: sun sensors, star trackers, magnetometers, IMUs, GPS.
- **Actuators**: reaction wheels (spin internal wheels to counter-rotate spacecraft), control moment gyros (CMGs), thrusters (RCS), magnetorquers (for LEO).
- **Software**: Kalman filter for state estimation, PID or modern control for tracking commands.

**Power**: solar arrays (most missions) + batteries (during eclipses). Plutonium-238 RTG for deep-space (Voyager, Cassini, Mars rovers, New Horizons).

**Thermal**: keep spacecraft within temperature limits (-100°C to +100°C typical). Vacuum + radiation + sun-shadow create huge gradients. Tools: MLI blankets, heat pipes, radiators, electric heaters, louvers.

**Communications**: link to ground stations.
- **Antennas**: high-gain dishes (deep-space), patch antennas (LEO).
- **Frequencies**: S-band (2 GHz, telemetry), X-band (8 GHz, deep-space), Ka-band (32 GHz, high-rate).
- **Tracking**: Deep Space Network (DSN) — 70m + 34m dishes worldwide for deep-space comms.

**Data + on-board computer**:
- Radiation-tolerant CPU (RAD750: 200 MHz, used in Mars Curiosity, JWST. ~\$200K each).
- Modern: RAD5500, ARM Cortex-A53 radiation-tolerant, FPGA-based.
- Latched-up state on radiation hit: SEU (Single Event Upset). Memory scrubbing + watchdog timers required.

**Payload**: the WORK the spacecraft does. Cameras, antennas, scientific instruments, communications relays. Everything else is 'bus' supporting the payload.

**ConOps (Concept of Operations)**: how the spacecraft will be operated. Mission timeline, contact schedule, safe modes, anomaly handling. Foundational document.

slides.title: Power budgeting
slides.body:
**Power budget**: each subsystem has nominal + peak power draw. Must be supplied by solar / RTG; stored in batteries.

**Typical LEO satellite power**:
- Communications: 10-100 W (depending on link power).
- Computers: 10-50 W.
- ADCS: 10-50 W (reaction wheels, sensors).
- Heaters: 10-100 W (peak when in shadow).
- Payload: 10-1000 W+.
- Total typical small sat (CubeSat): 10-100 W.
- Large communication sat: 5-25 kW.

**Solar arrays**:
- At Earth, solar flux 1361 W/m² (above atmosphere).
- Cell efficiency: 28-32% for triple-junction (modern), 18-22% for silicon.
- Useful output: 300-400 W/m² of array.
- Sun-tracking + sun pointing required.

**Eclipse**: in LEO, spacecraft in Earth's shadow ~30 min per 90-min orbit. Batteries supply during eclipse. Battery cycles: 16/day × 5+ years = 30,000+ cycles. Sizing for cycle depth + life is mission-critical.

**Battery types**:
- **NiCad**: legacy, robust.
- **NiH2**: Hubble Space Telescope (replaced 2002 with Li-ion).
- **Lithium-ion**: modern standard. Lighter, higher energy density. CYCLE-LIFE-LIMITED.

**At distance from sun**:
- Mars: 43% Earth's solar flux. Larger arrays needed.
- Jupiter: 4% Earth. RTGs preferred (Juno used solar; difficult).
- Saturn-Neptune: RTG mandatory.
- RTG: Pu-238 decay heat → thermoelectric conversion. ~100 W per kg of Pu-238. Multi-decade operation (Voyager-1 still operating 47 years after launch in 2024).

**Power management distribution**: regulators + busses + switches. Critical to avoid faults from rippling through system. Spacecraft typically have multiple redundant power paths.

slides.title: Thermal + comms + the complete system
slides.body:
**Thermal design**:
- Vacuum eliminates convection. Only radiation + conduction.
- Solar input + Earth IR + albedo on one side; deep-space cold sink on the other.
- Components must operate within thermal limits (e.g., electronics 0-50°C, batteries 0-30°C).

**Tools**:
- **MLI (Multi-Layer Insulation)**: gold-coated Kapton blankets, layered. Reduces radiative heat transfer. The 'gold foil' look of spacecraft.
- **Heat pipes**: capillary fluid moves heat from hot to cold parts.
- **Radiators**: large area facing deep space. Reject heat.
- **Electric heaters**: heat components if too cold.
- **Louvers / phase-change materials**: active or passive temperature control.

**Worst cases**:
- **Hot case**: subsolar point, eclipse exit, all heaters on, full sun.
- **Cold case**: deep eclipse, heaters failed, minimum power.
- Design must work at both extremes.

**Communications link budget**:
$$P_{\text{received}} = P_{\text{transmit}} \cdot G_{\text{tx}} \cdot G_{\text{rx}} / (L \cdot F^2)$$
where $G$ is antenna gain, $L$ is path loss, $F$ is frequency.

For deep-space:
- Voyager 1 (24 billion km from Earth as of 2024): transmits 23 W; signal received on DSN 70m dish is ~$10^{-19}$ W. Signal-to-noise around 1; data rate ~160 bps.
- DSN amplifiers: cryogenic, ultra-low-noise.
- Light delay: Voyager 1 ~22 hours one-way (delayed commands).

**Modern broadband from space**: Starlink (~12,000 sats), OneWeb (~600), Kuiper (in deployment) provide Mbps-Gbps to LEO. Phased-array antennas. Inter-satellite optical links (laser) for backbone routing.

**Total spacecraft system**:
- Bus (structure + power + thermal + comms + ADCS + propulsion + computer): ~50-70% of spacecraft mass.
- Payload (instruments, science, mission): rest.
- For commercial comsats: payload (transponders) is large fraction.
- For science (Hubble, JWST, planetary): payload dominates.

**Verification testing**: extensive ground testing in thermal-vacuum chambers, vibration test (launch loads), EMC (electromagnetic compatibility), software hardware-in-loop simulators. Months of testing before launch.

question.question: Design a satellite power budget
question.goal: LEO satellite. Avg power draw 50 W. Orbit period 95 min, eclipse 35 min. Battery efficiency 80%. Battery DoD 30% (depth-of-discharge limit for 5-year life).

steps.prompt: Eclipse energy required: 50 W × 35 min × 60 s/min = ?
Battery sized for 30% DoD: nominal capacity = 29.2 Wh / 0.30 = ?

Solar array sizing: must support load + recharge battery during sun-pass. Sun time 60 min (95 - 35). Charge needed: 29.2/0.80 = 36.5 Wh (efficiency loss). Plus continuing 50 W load. Required array power?
hints: 50 W load + 36.5 Wh / 1 hour = 36.5 W recharge → 86.5 W total.
steps.reveal: ~87 W during sun. Array might be sized at 100-120 W for margin + end-of-life degradation (~30% over 10 years from radiation).

question.finalResult: $$\boxed{\text{Power} = \text{Sun load} + \text{Battery recharge}}$$ Spacecraft power budgeting is multi-step: average load, eclipse energy, battery sizing (DoD + efficiency + cycle life), array sizing (load + recharge + EOL degradation). Each step has industry-standard margins. Spacecraft engineers spend significant effort on this; mis-sized power is a common mission-killer. Modern small-sat power design is increasingly aided by software tools (STK, FreeFlyer, Systems Tool Kit).

question.question: Voyager 1, ~24 billion km from Earth, sends radio signals at 23 W. Earth receives them. How?
options: Three things: (1) Voyager's high-gain antenna concentrates signal toward Earth; (2) DSN's 70-meter dishes are extremely sensitive; (3) cryogenic low-noise amplifiers + integration over time. Signal-to-noise is borderline; data rate ~160 bps with error correction.
question.explanation: Deep-space communications is signal-detection at the edge of physics. Voyager's 23W radiated → 70m DSN dish receives ~$10^{-19}$ W (less than one photon per bit). Cryogenic LNAs + integration time + error correction extract bits. Light delay: ~22 hours one-way. Data rate: 160 bps (yes, BPS — not kbps). Yet Voyager-1 still sends science data 47 years after launch. Engineering marvel. NASA tracks it with 70m antennas in California, Australia, Spain.

slides.workedSolution: $P_{rx} = P_{tx} \cdot G_{tx} \cdot G_{rx} / (4\pi d/\lambda)^2$. For Voyager: huge path loss but high gains + extreme sensitivity + integration over many seconds per bit. SNR around 1 with error correction. Engineering: focused transmitter + huge dishes + cryogenic amplifiers + low data rate. Modern Mars missions (~150-200 million km) get Mbps; Voyager (24 billion km) gets bps. Distance squared in the link equation is unforgiving.

CubeSat design
question.prompt: Designing a 3U CubeSat (30×10×10 cm) for Earth observation. Walk through the major subsystem trade-offs.
Explain in two or three sentences why spacecraft engineering is treated as a system-of-systems discipline rather than independent subsystem design.
question.rubric: Mentions that every subsystem couples to others (more power needs more solar array → more area → more thermal radiation → different attitude control → different propellant ...); mass-budget constraints make trade-offs critical; reliability requires careful interface management; the system engineer's role exists to manage these couplings. The cost of getting it wrong is mission failure on a $100M-$10B spacecraft.
